opening.text: Think about a cold night in the mountains. A group of hikers is huddled together. The wind is sharp. Someone strikes a match and lights a fire. At first it is small. But as the wood catches, the warmth spreads. Hands relax. Faces soften. People who were silent start to talk.
A fire does not ask who deserves to be warm. It simply gives heat to everyone near it.
That is a good picture of charity. It is a warmth that comes from Jesus Christ, and it reaches whoever is near.

mainMessage.text: Many of us think charity means giving money or old clothes to people in need. That is a good thing to do. But in the scriptures, charity means something deeper. It is the pure love of Christ. It is how He loves, and how He wants us to love.

This kind of love is not a feeling that comes and goes. It is a gift from God, and it changes who we are. When we have it, we treat people differently. We speak differently. We forgive more easily and serve more willingly.

We will look at six parts today. What charity is. Where it comes from. How it shows up in our words and habits. How it deals with others' faults. How it leads us to serve. And how it connects us to Christ.

blocks.text: Let us begin with the best description of charity in all of scripture. Mormon gave it to his people.

And charity suffereth long, and is kind, and envieth not, and is not puffed up, seeketh not her own, is not easily provoked, thinketh no evil, and rejoiceth not in iniquity but rejoiceth in the truth, beareth all things, believeth all things, hopeth all things, endureth all things.
Wherefore, my beloved brethren, if ye have not charity, ye are nothing, for charity never faileth. Wherefore, cleave unto charity, which is the greatest of all, for all things must fail—
But charity is the pure love of Christ, and it endureth forever; and whoso is found possessed of it at the last day, it shall be well with him.

Read those words slowly. Suffereth long. Is kind. Envieth not. Thinketh no evil. Beareth all things. Each phrase is a way of loving. And at the end, the definition. Charity is the pure love of Christ.
Paul said the same thing a few hundred years earlier.
And now abideth faith, hope, charity, these three; but the greatest of these is charity.
Faith, hope, and charity. Three gifts that go together. And the greatest is charity.
Elder Joseph B. Wirthlin of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles explained how these three work together. In his talk "Cultivating Divine Attributes," from the October 1998 general conference, he said:

Charity can be the outward expression of faith and hope. If sought and obtained, these three foundation elements of celestial character will abide with us in this life and beyond the veil into the next life.

The outward expression. That is a helpful way to see it. Faith and hope are what we hold inside. Charity is what people see. It is how our faith and hope show up in the way we treat others. Like a fire inside a cabin, you can tell it is lit by the warmth in the windows.
Where does this love come from? We cannot make a fire from nothing. We need a spark.
John gave the answer in plain words.
Herein is love, not that we loved God, but that he loved us, and sent his Son to be the propitiation for our sins. Beloved, if God so loved us, we ought also to love one another.

He loved us first. That is where the spark comes from. We do not have to build love from our own small supply. We receive it from God, and then we share it. Because He loved us, we ought also to love one another.
Elder Neal A. Maxwell of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles helped us see how big this love is. In his talk "Lessons from Laman and Lemuel," from the October 1999 general conference, he said:

The tree of life . . . is the love of God (see 1 Ne. 11:25). The love of God for His children is most profoundly expressed in His gift of Jesus as our Redeemer: 'God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son' (John 3:16). To partake of the love of God is to partake of Jesus' Atonement and the emancipations and joys which it can bring.
The tree of life is the love of God. When we partake of it, we are filled. And as we are filled, there is enough to share. A fire that has plenty of fuel can warm the whole camp.
So how do we receive more of it? Mormon told us.

Wherefore, my beloved brethren, pray unto the Father with all the energy of heart, that ye may be filled with this love, which he hath bestowed upon all who are true followers of his Son, Jesus Christ; that ye may become the sons of God; that when he shall appear we shall be like him, for we shall see him as he is; that we may have this hope; that we may be purified even as he is pure. Amen.
Pray with all the energy of heart. That is a lot of effort. Charity is a gift, but we are asked to ask for it, and to ask with real desire. And it is given to true followers of Christ.
Elder Wirthlin said more about this in the same talk, "Cultivating Divine Attributes." He said:

Note that charity is given only to those who seek it, only to those who earnestly pray for it, only to those who are disciples of Christ. Before we can be filled with this pure love, we must start at the beginning with the first principle of the gospel.

Given to those who seek it. That means we can ask. If you feel your love is small, or tired, or hard, you can pray for more. You can say, Father, help me love as Jesus does. That is a prayer He wants to answer.
What does this fire look like in daily life? Often it looks small. A kind word. A patient answer. A gentle correction.
Paul wrote to the saints in Colossae about how to dress our souls.

Put on therefore, as the elect of God, holy and beloved, bowels of mercies, kindness, humbleness of mind, meekness, longsuffering; Forbearing one another, and forgiving one another, if any man have a quarrel against any: even as Christ forgave you, so also do ye. And above all these things put on charity, which is the bond of perfectness.
Put on. Charity is like a coat. We choose to wear it. Mercy, kindness, humility, meekness, patience. And above all these, charity, which ties them all together.
He wrote a short version to the saints in Ephesus too.
And be ye kind one to another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, even as God for Christ's sake hath forgiven you.
Kind one to another. Tenderhearted. Forgiving. Those are the sparks that keep the fire going in a home, a ward, or a workplace.
Elder Marvin J. Ashton of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles gave a very practical picture. In his talk "The Tongue Can Be a Sharp Sword," from the April 1992 general conference, he said:

Perhaps the greatest charity comes when we are kind to each other, when we don't judge or categorize someone else, when we simply give each other the benefit of the doubt or remain quiet. Charity is accepting someone's differences, weaknesses, and shortcomings; having patience with someone who has let us down; or resisting the impulse to become offended when someone doesn't handle something the way we might have hoped. Charity is refusing to take advantage of another's weakness and being willing to forgive someone who has hurt us. Charity is expecting the best of each other.

Expecting the best of each other. That is simple to say and hard to do. But it can change a marriage, a family, a quorum, or a class. Giving someone the benefit of the doubt costs us nothing, and it can warm a very cold room.
Now a harder question. What does charity do when people are difficult? When they disappoint us, or when they are different from us?
A lot of us would like to love only the easy people. But the Savior set a higher mark. A man once asked Him which commandment was greatest. Jesus answered.

Jesus said unto him, Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy mind. This is the first and great commandment. And the second is like unto it, Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself. On these two commandments hang all the law and the prophets.
Two commandments. Love God. Love your neighbor. Everything else hangs on these. Like a coat on two hooks, the whole gospel hangs here.
And on the night before He died, Jesus added something.
A new commandment I give unto you, That ye love one another; as I have loved you, that ye also love one another. By this shall all men know that ye are my disciples, if ye have love one to another.
As I have loved you. That is the measure. Not as much as we feel like. As He has loved us. And that is how people will know who His disciples are. Not by our titles or our callings, but by our love.
President Dieter F. Uchtdorf of the First Presidency spoke about this in his talk "You Are My Hands," from the April 2010 general conference. He said:

I am not suggesting that we accept sin or overlook evil, in our personal life or in the world. Nevertheless, in our zeal, we sometimes confuse sin with sinner, and we condemn too quickly and with too little compassion. . . . Let our hearts and hands be stretched out in compassion toward others, for everyone is walking his or her own difficult path.

Everyone is walking a difficult path. That one sentence can soften a hard heart. The person who cut you off in traffic, the coworker who snapped at you, the child who is acting out. Each one is carrying something we cannot see. Compassion starts when we remember that. A fire does not lecture the cold. It just gives warmth.
What does charity lead us to do? It leads us to serve.
King Benjamin was a king who worked with his own hands. He told his people why.
And behold, I tell you these things that ye may learn wisdom; that ye may learn that when ye are in the service of your fellow beings ye are only in the service of your God.
When we serve our fellow beings, we are serving God. That makes every small act of service important. Carrying groceries. Visiting a neighbor. Making a meal. Showing up. To God, those are not small.
Jesus taught the same truth when He spoke about the final judgment.
And the King shall answer and say unto them, Verily I say unto you, Inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of the least of these my brethren, ye have done it unto me.
Inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of the least of these. The one who is hungry. The one who is lonely. The one who is overlooked. When we reach them, we have reached Him.
Charity does not wait for a big moment. A fire spreads by small sticks, one at a time. One visit. One phone call. One meal. One open door.
Where does all this lead? It leads us to Christ, and to be like Him.
Jesus showed us the highest form of love.
Greater love hath no man than this, that a man lay down his life for his friends.
He did that. He laid down His life for us. And He did it willingly, in an act of pure love.
Elder Wirthlin spoke about this in his talk "Christians in Belief and Action," from the October 1996 general conference. He said:

The Atonement of Jesus Christ, an act of pure love, overcame the effects of the Fall and provided the way for all mankind to return to the presence of God. As part of the Atonement, the Savior overcame physical death and provided immortality for every one of God's children through the Resurrection. He also overcame spiritual death and provided the possibility of eternal life, the life that God lives and the greatest of all the gifts of God.
An act of pure love. That is where charity comes from. It started with Him. And Moroni told us how much it matters.
And except ye have charity ye can in nowise be saved in the kingdom of God; neither can ye be saved in the kingdom of God if ye have not faith; neither can ye if ye have no hope.

Except ye have charity. That is a serious statement. Charity is not an extra. It is part of what makes us ready to live with God. And the good news is that it is a gift. We can ask for it. And as we use it, it grows.

story.prompt: The member tells a true time when they were shown, or showed, real kindness. If the member has none, the app offers a story from the scriptures.
story.title: The Good Samaritan

blocks.text: Jesus told a story about a man who was beaten and left on the road. A priest walked by. A Levite walked by. Then a Samaritan, someone the Jews looked down on, came upon him.

But a certain Samaritan, as he journeyed, came where he was: and when he saw him, he had compassion on him, And went to him, and bound up his wounds, pouring in oil and wine, and set him on his own beast, and brought him to an inn, and took care of him. And on the morrow when he departed, he took out two pence, and gave them to the host, and said unto him, Take care of him; and whatsoever thou spendest more, when I come again, I will repay thee.

Look at the verbs. He saw. He had compassion. He went to him. He bound up wounds. He set him on his own animal. He paid the bill. And he promised to come back. That is charity. It sees, it feels, and it acts. And it does not ask who the person is.

application.text: Here are some steps for this week.
First, ask for the gift. Each morning, pray Mormon's prayer in your own words. Ask the Father to fill you with the pure love of Christ. Do it for seven days and notice what changes.
Second, give the benefit of the doubt. Pick one person you find difficult. This week, when they annoy you, expect the best of them. Respond with kindness, even in a small way.
Third, light one fire. Choose one act of service for someone who cannot repay you. A meal, a ride, a visit. Do it quietly.

testimony.prompt: The member adds their own words. Lines the app offers:

blocks.text: I know that charity is the pure love of Christ. I know that He loved us first, and that He gives this love to all who ask with real desire. I have felt His love through the kindness of others, and I have felt it fill my own heart when I served. I know that this love never fails. I say these things in the name of Jesus Christ, amen.

invitations: I invite you to pray each morning this week for the pure love of Christ.
I invite you to give one person you find difficult the benefit of the doubt.
I invite you to do one quiet act of service for someone who cannot repay you.
blessings: You will be filled with the love of Christ.
Your heart will soften toward others.
You will become more like the Savior.

closingVerse.text: We love him, because he first loved us.

opening.text: There is a river near a small town. Years ago, the people on one side hardly knew the people on the other. The water was too wide. Then someone built a bridge. It was a plain bridge, made of timber. But everything changed. Neighbors visited. Children crossed to school. Families who had never met sat down at one table.
A bridge does not make the river smaller. It makes the distance crossable.
That is what charity does. It is the love that lets us cross over to one another.

mainMessage.text: There are many rivers between people. Differences in age, background, opinion, or pain. Sometimes the river is only a small quarrel. Sometimes it is years of silence. Charity is the bridge. It is the pure love of Christ, and it lets us reach those who seem far away.
The gospel teaches that this love is a gift. We do not build it alone. The Savior supplies the strength, and we supply the willingness.

Here are the six parts we will cover. What charity is. Where it begins. How it shapes our daily words. How it changes the way we see others. How it moves us to serve. And how it joins us to the Savior.

blocks.text: First, what is charity? Mormon spoke to his people about it in words we still read today.

And charity suffereth long, and is kind, and envieth not, and is not puffed up, seeketh not her own, is not easily provoked, thinketh no evil, and rejoiceth not in iniquity but rejoiceth in the truth, beareth all things, believeth all things, hopeth all things, endureth all things.
Wherefore, my beloved brethren, if ye have not charity, ye are nothing, for charity never faileth. Wherefore, cleave unto charity, which is the greatest of all, for all things must fail—
But charity is the pure love of Christ, and it endureth forever; and whoso is found possessed of it at the last day, it shall be well with him.

A long list of qualities. Patient. Kind. Not jealous. Not proud. Not selfish. Not quick to anger. Slow to think evil. These are the planks of the bridge. And then the plain definition. Charity is the pure love of Christ.
Paul wrote the same truth in a famous letter to the Corinthians.
And now abideth faith, hope, charity, these three; but the greatest of these is charity.
Of all the gifts, charity is the greatest. It is the one that lasts.

Elder Joseph B. Wirthlin of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles described how faith, hope, and charity fit together. In his talk "Cultivating Divine Attributes," from the October 1998 general conference, he said:

Charity can be the outward expression of faith and hope. If sought and obtained, these three foundation elements of celestial character will abide with us in this life and beyond the veil into the next life.

The outward expression. Faith and hope are the foundations on the banks of the river. Charity is the span in the middle that people actually walk across. It takes what we believe and puts it where others can use it.
Where does this bridge begin? On God's side of the river.
John wrote about this with great simplicity.
Herein is love, not that we loved God, but that he loved us, and sent his Son to be the propitiation for our sins. Beloved, if God so loved us, we ought also to love one another.
He first loved us. The first plank was laid by Him. He sent His Son. Because of that gift, we are able to cross over to Him. And since He has crossed to us, we ought to cross to each other.
Elder Neal A. Maxwell of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles spoke of how large that love is. In his talk "Lessons from Laman and Lemuel," from the October 1999 general conference, he said:

The tree of life . . . is the love of God (see 1 Ne. 11:25). The love of God for His children is most profoundly expressed in His gift of Jesus as our Redeemer: 'God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son' (John 3:16). To partake of the love of God is to partake of Jesus' Atonement and the emancipations and joys which it can bring.

To partake of the love of God is to partake of the Atonement. Think of that. The love of God and the Atonement are the same gift seen from two sides. And the joy that comes from it is meant to be shared.
How do we receive more? Mormon gave a plain instruction.

Wherefore, my beloved brethren, pray unto the Father with all the energy of heart, that ye may be filled with this love, which he hath bestowed upon all who are true followers of his Son, Jesus Christ; that ye may become the sons of God; that when he shall appear we shall be like him, for we shall see him as he is; that we may have this hope; that we may be purified even as he is pure. Amen.
Pray for it. With all the energy of heart. That is the way to strengthen the bridge. And the promise is large. We may become the sons and daughters of God. We shall be like Him.
Elder Wirthlin taught this in the same talk, "Cultivating Divine Attributes." He said:

Note that charity is given only to those who seek it, only to those who earnestly pray for it, only to those who are disciples of Christ. Before we can be filled with this pure love, we must start at the beginning with the first principle of the gospel.

The first principle of the gospel is faith in the Lord Jesus Christ. That is where the road begins. A person who is trying to follow Him and who asks for love will receive it. It is not reserved for the naturally kind. It is given to the willing.
How does charity shape our everyday words and habits? Often in ways no one else sees.
Paul gave a list of things to wear each day.

Put on therefore, as the elect of God, holy and beloved, bowels of mercies, kindness, humbleness of mind, meekness, longsuffering; Forbearing one another, and forgiving one another, if any man have a quarrel against any: even as Christ forgave you, so also do ye. And above all these things put on charity, which is the bond of perfectness.
The bond of perfectness. A bond holds things together. Charity is the bolt that holds the bridge to both banks. Without it, even the finest qualities can drift apart.
Paul gave the shortest version in his letter to the Ephesians.
And be ye kind one to another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, even as God for Christ's sake hath forgiven you.
Kind. Tenderhearted. Forgiving. If you want to know whether you have charity, ask yourself whether you are those three things on an ordinary Tuesday.

Elder Marvin J. Ashton of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles gave an honest look at how charity feels in daily life. In his talk "The Tongue Can Be a Sharp Sword," from the April 1992 general conference, he said:

Perhaps the greatest charity comes when we are kind to each other, when we don't judge or categorize someone else, when we simply give each other the benefit of the doubt or remain quiet. Charity is accepting someone's differences, weaknesses, and shortcomings; having patience with someone who has let us down; or resisting the impulse to become offended when someone doesn't handle something the way we might have hoped. Charity is refusing to take advantage of another's weakness and being willing to forgive someone who has hurt us. Charity is expecting the best of each other.

Or remain quiet. That is a gift too. Sometimes the most loving thing we can do is hold our tongue. And expecting the best is the plank that makes the whole bridge strong. People often become what we expect them to be.
Some rivers are wide. How do we love the people who are hard for us to love? How do we cross to someone who has hurt us, or who sees the world differently?
The Savior gave us the starting point. A lawyer asked Him to name the great commandment.

Jesus said unto him, Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy mind. This is the first and great commandment. And the second is like unto it, Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself. On these two commandments hang all the law and the prophets.

Love God. Love your neighbor. Those are the two ends of the bridge. If we are missing either one, we fall short of the other side. The second is like unto the first. Loving God and loving people go together.
And in the upper room, the night before the cross, Jesus gave a new commandment.
A new commandment I give unto you, That ye love one another; as I have loved you, that ye also love one another. By this shall all men know that ye are my disciples, if ye have love one to another.

As I have loved you. He is the engineer. He shows us how to build. His love was patient, steady, and generous, even to those who denied Him and left Him. And by this, He said, all men shall know that we are His disciples.
President Dieter F. Uchtdorf of the First Presidency gave a gentle reminder in his talk "You Are My Hands," from the April 2010 general conference. He said:

I am not suggesting that we accept sin or overlook evil, in our personal life or in the world. Nevertheless, in our zeal, we sometimes confuse sin with sinner, and we condemn too quickly and with too little compassion. . . . Let our hearts and hands be stretched out in compassion toward others, for everyone is walking his or her own difficult path.

President Uchtdorf is not telling us to give up what is right. He is telling us not to confuse sin with sinner. We can hold to our standards and still show compassion. When we remember that everyone is walking a difficult path, a crossing opens up where there was only water before.
What does a bridge do? It carries people across. Charity does the same. It moves us to serve.
King Benjamin worked with his hands to provide for his people. He wanted them to understand why.
And behold, I tell you these things that ye may learn wisdom; that ye may learn that when ye are in the service of your fellow beings ye are only in the service of your God.
When we serve our fellow beings, we serve our God. It is that direct. There is no step in between. The meal you take to a neighbor is a meal you take to Him.
Jesus said it Himself when He described the day of judgment.
And the King shall answer and say unto them, Verily I say unto you, Inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of the least of these my brethren, ye have done it unto me.

The least of these. It is not the powerful or the popular He mentions. It is the hungry, the stranger, the sick, the prisoner. The ones people walk past. When we stop for them, we are stopping for the Savior.
A bridge is built from many small pieces of wood. Each act of service is a plank. We may never see the whole bridge. But someone will cross it.
Where does charity lead us? To Christ, who is the bridge.
The Savior spoke about the highest love.
Greater love hath no man than this, that a man lay down his life for his friends.
He did exactly that. He gave everything for us. He became the bridge between God and man.
Elder Wirthlin spoke of this in his talk "Christians in Belief and Action," from the October 1996 general conference. He said:

The Atonement of Jesus Christ, an act of pure love, overcame the effects of the Fall and provided the way for all mankind to return to the presence of God. As part of the Atonement, the Savior overcame physical death and provided immortality for every one of God's children through the Resurrection. He also overcame spiritual death and provided the possibility of eternal life, the life that God lives and the greatest of all the gifts of God.
The way for all mankind to return to the presence of God. That is the bridge. It was an act of pure love. When we love others with that love, we help them find the way across.
And Moroni said how essential this is.
And except ye have charity ye can in nowise be saved in the kingdom of God; neither can ye be saved in the kingdom of God if ye have not faith; neither can ye if ye have no hope.
Even faith and hope are not enough without charity. They are the foundations, but charity is the span. We cannot reach the far shore without it.

story.prompt: The member tells a true time when someone crossed a gap to reach them, or when they crossed one for someone else. If the member has none, the app offers a story from the scriptures.
story.title: Ruth and Naomi

blocks.text: Naomi had lost her husband and both her sons. She decided to go back to her homeland, Bethlehem. She told her daughters-in-law to return to their own families. One of them, Ruth, would not go.

Entreat me not to leave thee, or to return from following after thee: for whither thou goest, I will go; and where thou lodgest, I will lodge: thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God: Where thou diest, will I die, and there will I be buried: the Lord do so to me, and more also, if ought but death part thee and me.

Ruth was from Moab. Naomi was an Israelite. There was a river of culture, religion, and loss between them. Ruth built a bridge with one sentence. Thy people shall be my people. She crossed over and stayed. That is charity. It does not wait for things to be easy. It chooses to stay beside someone in their hardest season.

application.text: Here are some steps for this week.
First, find your river. Think of one relationship where there is a gap. A family member. A coworker. A neighbor. Write down one small thing you could do to cross it.
Second, pray for the gift. Use Moroni 7:48 as your guide. Ask the Father to fill you with the pure love of Christ. Do it every day this week.
Third, lay one plank. Do one act of kindness for someone you do not know well. A note, a meal, or a ride. Do it without being asked.

testimony.prompt: The member adds their own words. Lines the app offers:

blocks.text: I know that the love of Christ is real, and that it crosses every river. I know that He is the bridge between us and the Father. I have felt that love reach me when I was far off, and I have felt it grow in me when I reached out to others. I know that charity never fails. I say these things in the name of Jesus Christ, amen.

invitations: I invite you to think of one relationship where there is a gap and write down one small step to cross it.
I invite you to pray every day this week for the gift of charity.
I invite you to do one kind act for someone you do not know well.
blessings: The gap will begin to close.
You will feel the Savior's love.

closingVerse.text: Bear ye one another’s burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ.

opening.text: In many villages around the world, the well is the heart of the place. Women and children walk there each morning with buckets. Travelers stop to drink. Farmers fill their jugs. Nobody asks for a ticket. Nobody checks whether you are worthy. The well just gives.
But a well has a secret. It does not make the water. It draws from a spring deep below. A well that is cut off from its spring runs dry.
Charity is like that. We can give love to others only if we are connected to the Source.

mainMessage.text: The gospel calls this source the pure love of Christ. It is the deepest kind of love there is. It does not depend on mood or merit. It flows from the Savior to us, and through us to others.
Some days our own love runs low. We get tired, hurt, or annoyed. That is when we need to remember where the water comes from. If we stay connected to Christ, we can keep giving without running dry.

We will look at six parts. What charity is. Where the water comes from. How it flows in daily life. How it reaches difficult people. How it shows up in service. And how it leads us back to the Savior.

blocks.text: Let us start with the way Mormon described charity. It is the fullest picture in scripture.

And charity suffereth long, and is kind, and envieth not, and is not puffed up, seeketh not her own, is not easily provoked, thinketh no evil, and rejoiceth not in iniquity but rejoiceth in the truth, beareth all things, believeth all things, hopeth all things, endureth all things.
Wherefore, my beloved brethren, if ye have not charity, ye are nothing, for charity never faileth. Wherefore, cleave unto charity, which is the greatest of all, for all things must fail—
But charity is the pure love of Christ, and it endureth forever; and whoso is found possessed of it at the last day, it shall be well with him.
Charity never faileth. A good well does not fail in a dry season. It endures. And whoso is found possessed of it at the last day, it shall be well with him. That is a promise worth reaching for.
Paul put charity at the top of the list.
And now abideth faith, hope, charity, these three; but the greatest of these is charity.
Faith, hope, and charity. All three matter. But the greatest is charity.
Elder Joseph B. Wirthlin of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles showed how they are tied together. In his talk "Cultivating Divine Attributes," from the October 1998 general conference, he said:

Charity can be the outward expression of faith and hope. If sought and obtained, these three foundation elements of celestial character will abide with us in this life and beyond the veil into the next life.

A well needs three things: a deep shaft, a clean spring, and a bucket. Faith is the shaft. Hope is the spring. Charity is the bucket, the part that lifts the water up so others can drink. Without it, the water stays below.
Where does the water come from? It comes from God.
John wrote a short and beautiful lesson on this.
Herein is love, not that we loved God, but that he loved us, and sent his Son to be the propitiation for our sins. Beloved, if God so loved us, we ought also to love one another.
Not that we loved God, but that He loved us. The spring is His. Long before we could love Him, He loved us. And because of that, we have something to give.
Elder Neal A. Maxwell of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles explained how deep it goes. In his talk "Lessons from Laman and Lemuel," from the October 1999 general conference, he said:

The tree of life . . . is the love of God (see 1 Ne. 11:25). The love of God for His children is most profoundly expressed in His gift of Jesus as our Redeemer: 'God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son' (John 3:16). To partake of the love of God is to partake of Jesus' Atonement and the emancipations and joys which it can bring.

To partake of the love of God. We drink. And when we have drunk deeply, we have something to share. Those who have never felt the love of God often struggle to give it. Those who have tasted it find it flows out of them without much effort.
How do we draw more? Mormon gave us the bucket.

Wherefore, my beloved brethren, pray unto the Father with all the energy of heart, that ye may be filled with this love, which he hath bestowed upon all who are true followers of his Son, Jesus Christ; that ye may become the sons of God; that when he shall appear we shall be like him, for we shall see him as he is; that we may have this hope; that we may be purified even as he is pure. Amen.
Pray with all the energy of heart. This is not a quick prayer. It is the prayer of someone who is thirsty. And the promise is that we will be filled.
Elder Wirthlin explained who receives this gift. In the same talk, "Cultivating Divine Attributes," he said:

Note that charity is given only to those who seek it, only to those who earnestly pray for it, only to those who are disciples of Christ. Before we can be filled with this pure love, we must start at the beginning with the first principle of the gospel.
Only to those who seek it. That is an invitation as much as a condition. Seek it. Pray for it. Follow Him. And it will be given.
How does the water flow in daily life? In the ordinary things we say and do.
Paul wrote about what a person filled with charity looks like.

Put on therefore, as the elect of God, holy and beloved, bowels of mercies, kindness, humbleness of mind, meekness, longsuffering; Forbearing one another, and forgiving one another, if any man have a quarrel against any: even as Christ forgave you, so also do ye. And above all these things put on charity, which is the bond of perfectness.
Mercy, kindness, humility, meekness, patience. Forbearing one another. Forgiving one another. And above all, charity. It is the thing that holds the other qualities in place.
Paul put it more briefly to the Ephesians.
And be ye kind one to another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, even as God for Christ's sake hath forgiven you.

Even as God for Christ's sake hath forgiven you. That is the reason. We forgive because we have been forgiven. We are kind because we have been shown kindness. The water we pour out is the water we have received.
Elder Marvin J. Ashton of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles described how this looks. In his talk "The Tongue Can Be a Sharp Sword," from the April 1992 general conference, he said:

Perhaps the greatest charity comes when we are kind to each other, when we don't judge or categorize someone else, when we simply give each other the benefit of the doubt or remain quiet. Charity is accepting someone's differences, weaknesses, and shortcomings; having patience with someone who has let us down; or resisting the impulse to become offended when someone doesn't handle something the way we might have hoped. Charity is refusing to take advantage of another's weakness and being willing to forgive someone who has hurt us. Charity is expecting the best of each other.

Notice how many of these are things we do not do. We do not judge. We do not categorize. We do not take offense. We do not take advantage. Sometimes the strongest charity is what we hold back. And then there is the active side. We give the benefit of the doubt. We forgive. We expect the best.
How does the water reach those who are hard to love? Some people come to the well with a sharp tongue or a cold heart. How do we serve them?
The Savior gave the standard. When asked what mattered most, He named two things.

Jesus said unto him, Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy mind. This is the first and great commandment. And the second is like unto it, Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself. On these two commandments hang all the law and the prophets.
First, God. Second, our neighbor. And the second is like unto the first. A person who truly loves God will want to love the people God loves.
On His last night with the Twelve, He raised the bar.
A new commandment I give unto you, That ye love one another; as I have loved you, that ye also love one another. By this shall all men know that ye are my disciples, if ye have love one to another.
As I have loved you. That is the new part. It is not enough to love as we love ourselves. We are asked to love as He loves. With patience, with mercy, and without conditions.
President Dieter F. Uchtdorf of the First Presidency gave a clear reminder of how to do this. In his talk "You Are My Hands," from the April 2010 general conference, he said:

I am not suggesting that we accept sin or overlook evil, in our personal life or in the world. Nevertheless, in our zeal, we sometimes confuse sin with sinner, and we condemn too quickly and with too little compassion. . . . Let our hearts and hands be stretched out in compassion toward others, for everyone is walking his or her own difficult path.

We condemn too quickly. That is an honest line. We see someone's behavior and decide who they are. But we only see a piece of the path. Compassion asks us to remember there is more we do not know. The well gives to the grumpy man the same as to the kind one.
A well exists to be used. And charity is meant to move. It moves us to serve.
King Benjamin taught his people about this when he was an old man. He had served them his whole life, and he said:
And behold, I tell you these things that ye may learn wisdom; that ye may learn that when ye are in the service of your fellow beings ye are only in the service of your God.

In the service of your fellow beings, ye are only in the service of your God. That changes how we look at an ordinary task. Helping a child with homework. Driving an elderly neighbor to an appointment. Sitting with a friend who is grieving. It is all service to God.
The Savior said it directly.
And the King shall answer and say unto them, Verily I say unto you, Inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of the least of these my brethren, ye have done it unto me.
Inasmuch. That small word is full of hope. Whenever we do it, even once, it counts. A cup of water given to a thirsty traveler is a gift to the Savior Himself.
A well does not give water only to the great. It gives to anyone who comes with a bucket. We can be that kind of well.
Where does charity lead us in the end? To the One who is the fountain of living water.
Jesus gave us a statement of love that has never been surpassed.
Greater love hath no man than this, that a man lay down his life for his friends.
He did this. He gave His life for us, freely, in love.
Elder Wirthlin taught of the Atonement in his talk "Christians in Belief and Action," from the October 1996 general conference. He said:

The Atonement of Jesus Christ, an act of pure love, overcame the effects of the Fall and provided the way for all mankind to return to the presence of God. As part of the Atonement, the Savior overcame physical death and provided immortality for every one of God's children through the Resurrection. He also overcame spiritual death and provided the possibility of eternal life, the life that God lives and the greatest of all the gifts of God.
An act of pure love. This is the spring that fills every well. When we love as He loved, we are drawing from the deepest source there is.
And Moroni reminds us how much is at stake.
And except ye have charity ye can in nowise be saved in the kingdom of God; neither can ye be saved in the kingdom of God if ye have not faith; neither can ye if ye have no hope.

Without charity, we cannot be saved in the kingdom of God. This is not meant to scare us. It is meant to show us how central charity is. It is how we become like Him. And it is how we are ready to live with Him.

story.prompt: The member tells a true time when someone served them humbly, or when they served another. If the member has none, the app offers a story from the scriptures.
story.title: Jesus washes the disciples' feet

blocks.text: On the night before He suffered, Jesus did something no one expected. He was the Master. He was their Lord. And yet He did the work of the lowest servant.

He riseth from supper, and laid aside his garments; and took a towel, and girded himself. After that he poureth water into a basin, and began to wash the disciples' feet, and to wipe them with the towel wherewith he was girded.

He poured water into a basin. He knelt. He washed the dust from the feet of His friends. One of them was about to betray Him. Another would deny Him. And He washed their feet anyway. That is charity. It serves those who do not deserve it, and it does so with humility. The Source of all living water bent down and poured it out.

application.text: Here are some steps to try this week.
First, drink first. Spend a few minutes each day reading about the Savior's love. Let it fill you before you try to give it away. A full well gives freely.
Second, wash a pair of feet. Think of one humble act of service you could do. Something that no one will notice. Wash a dish. Mow a lawn. Carry a bag. Do it with love.

Third, give someone the benefit of the doubt. This week, choose a person who tests your patience. When they do something that bothers you, assume the best. Remember that they are walking a difficult path.

blocks.text: I know that Jesus Christ is the source of all true love. I know that His love fills us and flows through us when we ask. I have felt His love in my own life, and I have seen it in the lives of others who serve. I know that charity never fails. I say these things in the name of Jesus Christ, amen.

closingVerse.text: Which now of these three, thinkest thou, was neighbour unto him that fell among the thieves? And he said, He that shewed mercy on him. Then said Jesus unto him, Go, and do thou likewise.

opening.text: Picture a long table set for a family dinner. There are more plates than people. Someone says, "Why so many?" And the answer is simple. "In case anyone comes by."
That kind of table says something. It says that there is room. It says that a stranger is welcome and a neighbor is expected. It says that love does not count heads before it sets the food down.
When I think of charity, I think of that table. Charity is the open seat. It is the pure love of Christ, made visible in how we make room for each other.

mainMessage.text: Charity is not only about big sacrifices. Most of the time it is about small invitations. Pull up a chair. Sit with me. Tell me how you are. It is the love that makes room.
This love comes from the Savior. He is the Host of the greatest table of all. He invites us to eat, and then He asks us to invite others.

We will cover six parts. What charity is. Who supplies it. How it fills our daily habits. How it makes room for people who are hard to welcome. How it moves us to serve. And how it prepares us for the feast with Him.

blocks.text: Let us begin with how scripture describes charity. Mormon gave the fullest picture.

And charity suffereth long, and is kind, and envieth not, and is not puffed up, seeketh not her own, is not easily provoked, thinketh no evil, and rejoiceth not in iniquity but rejoiceth in the truth, beareth all things, believeth all things, hopeth all things, endureth all things.
Wherefore, my beloved brethren, if ye have not charity, ye are nothing, for charity never faileth. Wherefore, cleave unto charity, which is the greatest of all, for all things must fail—
But charity is the pure love of Christ, and it endureth forever; and whoso is found possessed of it at the last day, it shall be well with him.

If ye have not charity, ye are nothing. That is how serious it is. And then comes the sentence that explains it all. Charity is the pure love of Christ. When we try to love like Him, we are doing charity.
Paul agreed. He ranked it at the top.
And now abideth faith, hope, charity, these three; but the greatest of these is charity.
Of the three, the greatest is charity. It is the one that has the most reach. It touches other people.
Elder Joseph B. Wirthlin of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles taught how these gifts relate. In his talk "Cultivating Divine Attributes," from the October 1998 general conference, he said:

Charity can be the outward expression of faith and hope. If sought and obtained, these three foundation elements of celestial character will abide with us in this life and beyond the veil into the next life.
What we believe, we show. A family who believes in Christ and hopes for His promises will end up setting an extra plate. Charity is faith and hope in action at the table.
Who supplies the food? Not us. The Savior does.
John wrote a short truth about where love begins.
Herein is love, not that we loved God, but that he loved us, and sent his Son to be the propitiation for our sins. Beloved, if God so loved us, we ought also to love one another.
He loved us first. We sit at His table because He invited us. And since He has been so generous, we ought to be generous too.

Elder Neal A. Maxwell of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles spoke of the love of God and the tree of life. In his talk "Lessons from Laman and Lemuel," from the October 1999 general conference, he said:

The tree of life . . . is the love of God (see 1 Ne. 11:25). The love of God for His children is most profoundly expressed in His gift of Jesus as our Redeemer: 'God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son' (John 3:16). To partake of the love of God is to partake of Jesus' Atonement and the emancipations and joys which it can bring.
To partake. That is a table word. We partake of the fruit. We eat and are filled. And what we are filled with is the love of God, which came to us through the Atonement. It is the best meal there is.
How do we get more? Mormon told us to ask.

Wherefore, my beloved brethren, pray unto the Father with all the energy of heart, that ye may be filled with this love, which he hath bestowed upon all who are true followers of his Son, Jesus Christ; that ye may become the sons of God; that when he shall appear we shall be like him, for we shall see him as he is; that we may have this hope; that we may be purified even as he is pure. Amen.
Pray with all the energy of heart. The prayer of a hungry person. And the promise is that we will be filled, and in time we will become like Him.
Elder Wirthlin said more on this in "Cultivating Divine Attributes." He said:

Note that charity is given only to those who seek it, only to those who earnestly pray for it, only to those who are disciples of Christ. Before we can be filled with this pure love, we must start at the beginning with the first principle of the gospel.
Only to those who seek it. This is a gentle reminder that we have a part. The Lord has set the table, but we have to come and sit down. We seek, we pray, we follow Him. And we are filled.
How does charity show up at our daily tables, so to speak? In words and small acts.
Paul wrote to the saints in Colossae with a list of things to put on each day.

Put on therefore, as the elect of God, holy and beloved, bowels of mercies, kindness, humbleness of mind, meekness, longsuffering; Forbearing one another, and forgiving one another, if any man have a quarrel against any: even as Christ forgave you, so also do ye. And above all these things put on charity, which is the bond of perfectness.
The bond of perfectness. It is the tablecloth that ties the whole setting together. Kindness, mercy, humility, patience, and forgiveness all sit better when charity holds them.
He repeated the idea in a shorter form to the Ephesians.
And be ye kind one to another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, even as God for Christ's sake hath forgiven you.
Kind. Tenderhearted. Forgiving. If a home had those three, it would be a good place to live.
Elder Marvin J. Ashton of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles spoke about how this works in real life. In his talk "The Tongue Can Be a Sharp Sword," from the April 1992 general conference, he said:

Perhaps the greatest charity comes when we are kind to each other, when we don't judge or categorize someone else, when we simply give each other the benefit of the doubt or remain quiet. Charity is accepting someone's differences, weaknesses, and shortcomings; having patience with someone who has let us down; or resisting the impulse to become offended when someone doesn't handle something the way we might have hoped. Charity is refusing to take advantage of another's weakness and being willing to forgive someone who has hurt us. Charity is expecting the best of each other.

Think about the dinner table in your home. Does it feel like a place where people can be themselves? Where they will not be judged for a spill, a poor grade, or a bad day? That is charity. It is a table where everyone is expected to be at their best, and loved even when they are not.
Some guests are easy to seat. Others take more effort. How do we make room for the person who is hard to welcome?
When a man asked the Savior which commandment was the greatest, He gave two. One about God. One about people.

Jesus said unto him, Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy mind. This is the first and great commandment. And the second is like unto it, Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself. On these two commandments hang all the law and the prophets.

Thy neighbour. Not the neighbor who agrees with us. Not the one who waves back. The neighbor, whoever is near. The second commandment is like unto the first. If we love God, we make room at the table for the ones He loves.
Then, at the last supper, Jesus gave a new commandment.
A new commandment I give unto you, That ye love one another; as I have loved you, that ye also love one another. By this shall all men know that ye are my disciples, if ye have love one to another.

As I have loved you. At that very table, He had broken bread with the one who would betray Him. He had washed the feet of the one who would deny Him. He knew, and He loved anyway. That is the example we are given.
President Dieter F. Uchtdorf of the First Presidency spoke about this in his talk "You Are My Hands," from the April 2010 general conference. He said:

I am not suggesting that we accept sin or overlook evil, in our personal life or in the world. Nevertheless, in our zeal, we sometimes confuse sin with sinner, and we condemn too quickly and with too little compassion. . . . Let our hearts and hands be stretched out in compassion toward others, for everyone is walking his or her own difficult path.

We can hold to what is right and still make room. President Uchtdorf draws that line clearly. We do not accept sin. But we do not confuse the sin with the sinner. And we stretch out our hands. A stretched-out hand is how you pull up a chair for someone.
A table is not only for sitting. It is for serving. And charity moves us to give.
King Benjamin was a king who worked in the fields beside his people. He wanted them to know why.
And behold, I tell you these things that ye may learn wisdom; that ye may learn that when ye are in the service of your fellow beings ye are only in the service of your God.
In the service of your fellow beings. A meal is service. A ride is service. A listening ear is service. And each one is a gift to God Himself.
Jesus taught the same in a parable of the final judgment. He spoke of the hungry, the thirsty, the stranger, the sick, and the prisoner.
And the King shall answer and say unto them, Verily I say unto you, Inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of the least of these my brethren, ye have done it unto me.
Inasmuch as ye have done it. That is the table talk of heaven. It is not about large gifts. It is about whether we noticed. Whether we stopped. Whether we made room.
If you want to practice charity, look for the one who is eating alone, the one who is new, or the one whom no one has invited. Pull up a chair.
What is the end of this road? A feast with the Savior, and a heart made like His.
Jesus taught us what love looks like at its highest.
Greater love hath no man than this, that a man lay down his life for his friends.
He did lay down His life. And He did it in love, for each of us by name.
Elder Wirthlin taught about this gift in his talk "Christians in Belief and Action," from the October 1996 general conference. He said:

The Atonement of Jesus Christ, an act of pure love, overcame the effects of the Fall and provided the way for all mankind to return to the presence of God. As part of the Atonement, the Savior overcame physical death and provided immortality for every one of God's children through the Resurrection. He also overcame spiritual death and provided the possibility of eternal life, the life that God lives and the greatest of all the gifts of God.
The way for all mankind to return to the presence of God. That is an invitation to the biggest table of all. Because of His love, the door is open to everyone.
And Moroni said what must go with us when we come.
And except ye have charity ye can in nowise be saved in the kingdom of God; neither can ye be saved in the kingdom of God if ye have not faith; neither can ye if ye have no hope.
Charity, faith, and hope. These three are the invitation we carry to the table. And of those, charity is the one that most shows who we are following.

story.prompt: The member tells a true time when someone gave all they could, or when they did. If the member has none, the app offers a story from the scriptures.
story.title: The widow's two mites

blocks.text: Jesus once sat near the temple treasury and watched people put in their offerings. Many rich people gave large amounts. Then a poor widow came.

And Jesus sat over against the treasury, and beheld how the people cast money into the treasury: and many that were rich cast in much. And there came a certain poor widow, and she threw in two mites, which make a farthing. And he called unto him his disciples, and saith unto them, Verily I say unto you, That this poor widow hath cast more in, than all they which have cast into the treasury: For all they did cast in of their abundance; but she of her want did cast in all that she had, even all her living.

Two small coins. Almost nothing. But Jesus said she gave more than all the rest. Why? Because charity is measured by the heart, not the amount. The rich gave from their abundance. She gave from her want. When we give with love, even what seems small, it can be a feast in heaven's eyes. You do not need much to set an extra plate.

application.text: Here are some steps for this week.
First, set an extra plate. Invite someone to a meal or a visit. It might be a neighbor, a new member, or someone who lives alone. The invitation itself is the gift.
Second, give from what you have. Do not wait until you have more time or money. Choose one small thing that you can give this week. Two mites are enough.
Third, pray for a heart that makes room. Use Mormon's words. Ask to be filled with the pure love of Christ. Then watch for the people He puts in your path.

blocks.text: I know that Jesus Christ is the host of the greatest feast of all. I know that His love makes room for everyone. I have felt a seat made for me at His table, and I have seen how that love changes people. I know that charity never fails. I say these things in the name of Jesus Christ, amen.

opening.text: It is a cold morning. A boy is waiting at a bus stop in a thin jacket. His arms are crossed. His teeth are chattering. A woman standing nearby notices. She does not say much. She takes off her scarf and wraps it around his neck. He looks up, surprised. She smiles. The bus comes. That is all.
But the boy will remember it. A small piece of cloth. A moment of warmth. Someone saw him and did something.
That is what charity looks like. It is the pure love of Christ, moving through ordinary people, one scarf at a time.

mainMessage.text: We often think charity is a big thing. A grand gift. A sacrifice that gets noticed. But most of the time, charity is quiet. It is a scarf. It is a kind word at the right moment. It is paying attention to the person next to us.
This love is not something we invent. It is a gift from God, given to those who seek it. It shapes how we talk, how we listen, and how we treat people who are not easy to love.
We will cover six parts. What charity is. Where it comes from. How it shows up in daily habits. How it handles hard people. How it leads us to serve. And how it connects us to the Savior.

blocks.text: Let us start with a clear definition. Mormon gave one to his people.

And charity suffereth long, and is kind, and envieth not, and is not puffed up, seeketh not her own, is not easily provoked, thinketh no evil, and rejoiceth not in iniquity but rejoiceth in the truth, beareth all things, believeth all things, hopeth all things, endureth all things.
Wherefore, my beloved brethren, if ye have not charity, ye are nothing, for charity never faileth. Wherefore, cleave unto charity, which is the greatest of all, for all things must fail—
But charity is the pure love of Christ, and it endureth forever; and whoso is found possessed of it at the last day, it shall be well with him.

The pure love of Christ. That is the plain answer. All the other phrases, suffering long, being kind, not envying, not being easily provoked, are ways that love shows itself. A person with charity is patient with others and gentle in thought.
Paul placed it above every other gift.
And now abideth faith, hope, charity, these three; but the greatest of these is charity.
The greatest of these is charity. Not because faith and hope are less. But because charity is how they reach other people.
Elder Joseph B. Wirthlin of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles said this plainly. In his talk "Cultivating Divine Attributes," from the October 1998 general conference, he said:

Charity can be the outward expression of faith and hope. If sought and obtained, these three foundation elements of celestial character will abide with us in this life and beyond the veil into the next life.
The outward expression. Faith and hope are what we wear underneath. Charity is the coat that people can see. And like a good coat, it keeps others warm too.
Where does this love come from? Not from us.
John explained it in two verses.
Herein is love, not that we loved God, but that he loved us, and sent his Son to be the propitiation for our sins. Beloved, if God so loved us, we ought also to love one another.
He loved us first. The warmth we have was given to us. And so we ought to pass it on. The woman at the bus stop was not the source of warmth. She was just a carrier of what she had received.
Elder Neal A. Maxwell of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles described what that love is. In his talk "Lessons from Laman and Lemuel," from the October 1999 general conference, he said:

The tree of life . . . is the love of God (see 1 Ne. 11:25). The love of God for His children is most profoundly expressed in His gift of Jesus as our Redeemer: 'God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son' (John 3:16). To partake of the love of God is to partake of Jesus' Atonement and the emancipations and joys which it can bring.
To partake of the love of God is to partake of Jesus' Atonement. The love and the Atonement are the same gift. When we feel forgiven, we feel loved. When we feel loved, we are able to love.
How do we ask for more? Mormon gave a simple direction.

Wherefore, my beloved brethren, pray unto the Father with all the energy of heart, that ye may be filled with this love, which he hath bestowed upon all who are true followers of his Son, Jesus Christ; that ye may become the sons of God; that when he shall appear we shall be like him, for we shall see him as he is; that we may have this hope; that we may be purified even as he is pure. Amen.
All the energy of heart. This is a prayer with effort in it. And the promise at the end is large. We may be purified even as He is pure.
Elder Wirthlin said more about who can receive this gift. In the same talk, "Cultivating Divine Attributes," he said:

Note that charity is given only to those who seek it, only to those who earnestly pray for it, only to those who are disciples of Christ. Before we can be filled with this pure love, we must start at the beginning with the first principle of the gospel.
Only to those who seek it. That is a kind invitation. It says the door is open. If you want more love, ask for it, and keep following Christ.
How does charity show up in the small habits of daily life? In what we put on each morning.
Paul used the picture of clothing. It fits well with our coat.

Put on therefore, as the elect of God, holy and beloved, bowels of mercies, kindness, humbleness of mind, meekness, longsuffering; Forbearing one another, and forgiving one another, if any man have a quarrel against any: even as Christ forgave you, so also do ye. And above all these things put on charity, which is the bond of perfectness.
Put on. We choose what we wear. Mercy, kindness, humility, meekness, patience. And above all these things, charity, which holds them together like the stitching in a coat.
He gave a shorter version to the Ephesians.
And be ye kind one to another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, even as God for Christ's sake hath forgiven you.
Kind, tenderhearted, forgiving. We can put those on before we walk out the door.
Elder Marvin J. Ashton of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles described how it looks day to day. In his talk "The Tongue Can Be a Sharp Sword," from the April 1992 general conference, he said:

Perhaps the greatest charity comes when we are kind to each other, when we don't judge or categorize someone else, when we simply give each other the benefit of the doubt or remain quiet. Charity is accepting someone's differences, weaknesses, and shortcomings; having patience with someone who has let us down; or resisting the impulse to become offended when someone doesn't handle something the way we might have hoped. Charity is refusing to take advantage of another's weakness and being willing to forgive someone who has hurt us. Charity is expecting the best of each other.

Patience with someone who has let us down. Resisting the impulse to be offended. These are the quiet kinds of charity that nobody applauds. But they keep a home warm. They keep a ward warm. And they keep a heart from freezing over.
What if the person who is cold is the one we find hardest to like? What if they have been unkind to us?
Jesus knew we would face this. When He was asked to name the greatest commandment, He did not give one answer. He gave two.

Jesus said unto him, Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy mind. This is the first and great commandment. And the second is like unto it, Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself. On these two commandments hang all the law and the prophets.
Love God. Love your neighbor as yourself. That second one is not optional. It is like unto the first. A person who loves God cannot ignore the people God made.
And on the night before His death, He gave a new commandment.
A new commandment I give unto you, That ye love one another; as I have loved you, that ye also love one another. By this shall all men know that ye are my disciples, if ye have love one to another.

As I have loved you. That is the standard. He loved those who mocked Him. He loved those who left Him. And He asks us to love in the same way. The sign of a disciple is not a badge or a title. It is love.
President Dieter F. Uchtdorf of the First Presidency spoke about how to do this. In his talk "You Are My Hands," from the April 2010 general conference, he said:

I am not suggesting that we accept sin or overlook evil, in our personal life or in the world. Nevertheless, in our zeal, we sometimes confuse sin with sinner, and we condemn too quickly and with too little compassion. . . . Let our hearts and hands be stretched out in compassion toward others, for everyone is walking his or her own difficult path.

Everyone is walking a difficult path. The grumpy neighbor may be grieving. The rude clerk may be exhausted. The teenager who snaps may be afraid. We do not know. But when we assume there is a story behind the behavior, it is easier to hand them a scarf.
What does charity do next? It serves.
King Benjamin taught his people about service. He had spent his life in the service of others, and he wanted them to understand why.
And behold, I tell you these things that ye may learn wisdom; that ye may learn that when ye are in the service of your fellow beings ye are only in the service of your God.
When we serve people, we serve God. When the woman gave her scarf to the boy, she was in the service of her God. She may not have thought of it that way. But it was true.
Jesus described this in a parable about the final judgment.
And the King shall answer and say unto them, Verily I say unto you, Inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of the least of these my brethren, ye have done it unto me.

The least of these. It is a phrase that should make us look around. Who in our reach is the least? The one in the thin jacket. The one without a ride. The one without an invitation. When we help them, we help Him.
Charity does not have to be large. It only has to be real.
Where does all this lead? To the Savior, who gave us the greatest gift.
He described the highest love in a single line.
Greater love hath no man than this, that a man lay down his life for his friends.
He did exactly that. He gave His life for us, not because we were perfect, but because He loved us.
Elder Wirthlin spoke of this love in his talk "Christians in Belief and Action," from the October 1996 general conference. He said:

The Atonement of Jesus Christ, an act of pure love, overcame the effects of the Fall and provided the way for all mankind to return to the presence of God. As part of the Atonement, the Savior overcame physical death and provided immortality for every one of God's children through the Resurrection. He also overcame spiritual death and provided the possibility of eternal life, the life that God lives and the greatest of all the gifts of God.
An act of pure love. Think of all He gave. He did it so we could come home. And now He asks us to carry that love to others.
Moroni reminds us why it matters so much.
And except ye have charity ye can in nowise be saved in the kingdom of God; neither can ye be saved in the kingdom of God if ye have not faith; neither can ye if ye have no hope.
Charity, faith, and hope. All three. We need all three to be ready to live with God. And the one that most shows who we follow is charity.

story.prompt: The member tells a true time when they were given something they needed, or gave it. If the member has none, the app offers a story from the scriptures.
story.title: David and Jonathan

blocks.text: Jonathan was the son of King Saul. He could have become king one day. David was a young shepherd who had just defeated Goliath. By the usual rules, they might have been rivals. Instead, they became friends.

Then Jonathan and David made a covenant, because he loved him as his own soul. And Jonathan stripped himself of the robe that was upon him, and gave it to David, and his garments, even to his sword, and to his bow, and to his girdle.

He loved him as his own soul. And he showed it by giving. He took off his own robe and handed it over. Not a small gift. It was a prince's robe, and he gave it freely. Charity does not guard what it has. It gives, and it is glad to do it.

application.text: Here are some steps for this week.
First, carry a scarf. Look for one chance each day to give something small. A kind word. A ride. A smile. A few minutes of listening. Do it without being asked.
Second, pray for the gift. Use Moroni 7:48 as your prayer. Ask to be filled with the pure love of Christ. Then watch for who the Lord puts in your path.
Third, choose compassion. Think of one person who is hard to love. Remember that they are walking a difficult path. Do one kind thing for them this week.

testimony.prompt: The member adds their own words. Lines the app offers:

blocks.text: I know that charity is the pure love of Christ, and that it never fails. I know that He gave everything for us, and that He asks us to share that love with others. I have felt His warmth through the small kindnesses of others. I know that those who seek this gift will receive it. I say these things in the name of Jesus Christ, amen.
